title: Touring the South: Jimmy Rushing's white socks and the Chattanooga cop
summary: Only Cab and Duke could afford Pullmans. With Moten in Beaumont a man made Jimmy Rushing remove white socks at gunpoint. In Chattanooga a friendly Irish cop let Barefield walk at night.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Of course, the -- you know, as you were saying before on the -- when we were taping -- the smartest thing was the pullman in your own cars and the --
If you could -- well, Cab could afford that. Yeah, Cab and Duke could afford that.
But otherwise it was -- the musicians didn't want to go down South.

Well, I went down there with Benny Moten's band. We traveled all through -- in fact, that was our stomping ground, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas, Little Rock, Arkansas, and I went down there with Fletcher, and, well, you know, you just know where to go and where to stay.

I remember one time Benny Moten's band played at Beaumont, Texas, and Jimmy Rushing was sitting on the bandstand with white socks on, and a guy walked up there and pulled out his gun and said, 'Nigger, take those white socks off.'

I mean, so this kind of thing must have -- well, actually must have inspired feelings of frustration and hatred and all that, but it must have also, you know, you must have looked at those people and said how silly --
Well, some of them -- well, some of them were funny.
Some of it was funny. I mean --
-- some of it was very funny, and plus, it always happened -- I remember when I was living in Chattanooga --
Uh-huh, when you were sick that time.

Yeah. If you were -- you couldn't walk the streets at night if you were black, but I happened to know the cop on the beat, an Irish cop, and I could walk all through, used to walk, hey, Eddie, how you doing, everything,

never bothered me. But it was -- any other -- most Negroes in the town or some of the strange ones walk through there, he let me by because I was a musician and, you know, had some kind of -- but a lot of guys, they'd put you in jail, and cost you $2.00 to get out the next day.
